title.rendered: Introduction: The River Beneath The River

content.rendered:
In the late fall of 2015, Bruce Springsteen released The Ties That Bind: The River Collection, a lavish celebratory retrospective of a classic double album.

The package included such gems as a breathtaking, four-hour live concert film and the legendary, abandoned ten-track single album Bruce pulled back from the pressing plant in late 1979.

But for those who (like me) have spent decades tracking Springsteen’s artistic journey through bootlegs and studio logs, the real treasure of that box are the two dozen outtakes that revealed an artist writing at an almost frightening clip.

It was proof of what diehard fans had known for thirty-five years: Bruce’s songwriting for his fifth album, didn’t just yield a river. It produced a flood.

For every masterpiece that claimed a home on the official twenty-song sequence, two or three equally compelling candidates were cut, tinkered with, shelved, cannibalized for parts, or cast aside.

What makes these discarded tracks so essential—and why they warrant their own dedicated volume—is that they do not sound like typical studio rejects. These are not half-hearted filler cuts or throwaway jams. Songs like “Roulette,” “Loose Ends,” “Where the Bands Are,” “Restless Nights,” and “Be True” carry the melodic polish and lyrical bite of an alternate timeline’s greatest hits.

If we listen closely we begin to see the kaleidoscope of paths Bruce chose not to take.

In one direction lay the tight, power-pop perfection of a record that could have gone toe-to-toe with early Tom Petty or The Knack (“Take ’Em as They Come,” “I Wanna Be With You”).

In another lay the roots-rock revivalism of an East Coast bar band channeling Buddy Holly and King Curtis late on a Saturday night (“Paradise by the ‘C'”, “From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come”).

And lurking in the shadows are the paranoia-soaked political warnings (“Roulette”) and domestic autopsies (“Stray Bullet”) that show how Bruce was already steering toward the barrenness of Nebraska.

The essays collected in this companion volume examine that shadow catalog. Originally published on my now defunct E Street Shuffle blog, these “Roll of the Dice” entries explore the songs that fall outside the borders of the original 1980 release.

In addition to the songs included in the box set, you’ll also find spotlights on circulating rehearsal sessions and soundchecks that to this day have never seen any kind of official release or live performance.

In these works in progress, we catch Bruce mumbling placeholder phrases, testing drum tempos with Max Weinberg, or lifting welding abandoned riffs onto entirely new lyrics. It’s a fascinating window into Bruce’s songwriting process, even when the audio on these tracks is too muddy to invite repeat listening.

The River tells a story about adulthood, time, and the cost of the compromises we make. But the river beneath The River tells an equally vital story about the creative fire of the artist who forged it.

Let’s explore the vault.

© November 1, 2026

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Clarks: The River
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Clarks transform "The River" from ballad to full-on rocker, and it works--better than one might imagine was possible.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Angelyne
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: A cover that was almost a team-up in a parallel universe version of "The River" -- Gary U.S. Bonds and Steve Van Zandt replaced Bruce's original vocals on this outtake from the River recording sessions.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The River
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Into the river we dive, as we appreciate one of Bruce's finest and most heartbreaking songs.

jetpack-related-posts.title: You Can Look (But You Better Not Touch)
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In any arrangement and any style, "You Can Look" is guaranteed to bring the fun to any show it appears in. Let's trace its long and winding evolution inside.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Price You Pay
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: "The Price You Pay" is considered to be one of Bruce's most enigmatic songs, but it's only the backstory that's mysterious--the song reveals itself when we pay close attention.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Roll of the Dice: Meeting Across the River
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Whether you take it seriously or comedically, "Meeting Across the River" ranks high in Bruce's catalog and represents a leap forward in his songwriting. Insights, early versions, and rare performances inside.
